PHSCS 587

Reading a technical figure

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows a repeatable path from a scientific figure to a testable explanation

Start with the physical question the material answers. Identify what the figure represents, where its boundaries are, which direction each axis increases and what each line or region means. Translate one visible feature into a sentence before reaching for an equation: for example, particles diffuse down a concentration gradient.

For each equation, name every symbol, its unit, its location in the figure and whether it is an input, a derived quantity or a boundary condition. Record the assumptions that make the relation valid. Check dimensions and a limiting case, such as zero field, zero excess generation, a very wide well or a fully ionized bulk. These checks connect the mathematical expression to a physical prediction.

A small-parameter limit gives an equation a physical check. First isolate a dimensionless quantity x, then use (1 + x)^a ≈ 1 + ax when |x| is much smaller than one. Keep the first-order term through the algebra: it may be the term that carries the measurable change. In a donor-occupation calculation, substituting a positive dimensionless exponential for the Fermi-energy dependence can turn the equation into a quadratic; select a physically positive root before taking its logarithm.

For an energy-axis calculation, kBT ln(NC/ND) has units of energy because NC/ND is dimensionless. Multiplying by another energy factor would give energy squared, which flags a dimensional inconsistency before plotting. Choosing EC as the common energy reference makes a graph of EF − EC particularly easy to interpret.

Then explain the same idea to an imagined learner using the figure as the reference. Pose a small change to one input and predict its consequence before calculating. If the prediction is unclear, turn that gap into a specific question to resolve from the source. Active reconstruction and a fresh example provide stronger evidence of understanding than recognition while rereading.

Example

For D/μ = kBT/q, first identify diffusion coefficient and mobility. Their ratio has units volts, matching energy per charge. Then ask whether the nondegenerate, low-field, uniform-temperature assumptions hold before applying the relation to a highly injected contact.

Sources and scope
  • Reading, How to Study, pp. 1–2
  • PHSCS 587, Physics Hw1 recording 1: controlled expansions, exponential substitutions and root selection.

Practice

1. What is a useful next question when a formula’s symbols are familiar but its physical role is unclear?

Return to the figure and required prediction.

Ask which measured or predicted feature the formula controls, which inputs can change it, and which boundary or approximation makes the relationship valid.
